text: Staking means locking tokens into a contract so the protocol can rely on them — as security collateral, a liquidity commitment, or simply a demand sink it wants to reward. The reward compensates for two things you give up: liquidity, since tokens are locked, and risk, from slashing, smart-contract bugs, or token-price moves.

The basic formula is simple accrual: staked amount times rate times time. 1,000 tokens at a 10% annual rate for 90 days works out to 1,000 times 0.10 times 90 over 365, or about 24.66 tokens. The rate applies to your original principal the whole time — nothing compounds yet.

APR is that simple, non-compounding yearly rate. APY accounts for compounding, where each reward gets added to principal and starts earning its own reward. A 10% APR compounded daily actually realizes about 10.516% APY; compounded monthly, about 10.471%. With no compounding at all, APY equals APR exactly.

The more frequently rewards compound, the bigger the gap between the advertised APR and the APY you actually realize — which is exactly why auto-compounding vaults exist as their own product, which Lesson 17 covers.

The lifecycle runs stake, lock or bond, earn rewards per the emission schedule, then unbond — a cooldown period, often days to weeks, before tokens are liquid again, specifically so the system can't be drained instantly in a panic. Then withdrawal returns principal plus rewards.

On proof-of-stake networks, staking isn't risk-free — validators who misbehave can have a portion of their stake slashed, permanently destroyed, and delegators usually share that loss. Any advertised APY is a gross number that doesn't price in slashing, contract risk, or illiquidity. Next: yield farming and how incentive design builds on this.
